1: ---
2: name: frontend-design
3: description: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
4: license: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt
5: ---
6: 
7: # Frontend Design
8: 
9: Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.
10: 
11: ## Ground your designs in the subject matter
12: 
13: If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.
14: 
15: ## Design principles
16: 
17: For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.
18: 
19: Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.
20: 
21: Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.
22: 
23: Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.
24: 
25: Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
26: - Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
27: - Using all caps for labels.
28: - Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.
29: 
30: Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.
31: 
32: Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.
33: 
34: Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.
35: 
36: ## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique
37: 
38: For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
39: 1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
40: 2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
41: 3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
42: 4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
43: 5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.
44: 
45: All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.
46: 
47: Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
48: - Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
49: - Type: the typefaces and their roles.
50: - Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
51: - Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.
52: 
53: Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.
54: 
55: When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.
56: 
57: ## Restraint and self-critique
58: 
59: Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.
60: 
61: ## More on writing in design
62: 
63: Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.
64: 
65: Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.
66: 
67: Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.
68: 
69: Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.
70: 
71: Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

1: ---
2: name: webapp-testing
3: description: Toolkit for interacting with and testing local web applications using Playwright. Supports verifying frontend functionality, debugging UI behavior, capturing browser screenshots, and viewing browser logs.
4: license: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt
5: ---
6: 
7: # Web Application Testing
8: 
9: To test local web applications, write native Python Playwright scripts.
10: 
11: **Helper Scripts Available**:
12: - `scripts/with_server.py` - Manages server lifecycle (supports multiple servers)
13: 
14: **Always run scripts with `--help` first** to see usage. DO NOT read the source until you try running the script first and find that a customized solution is abslutely necessary. These scripts can be very large and thus pollute your context window. They exist to be called directly as black-box scripts rather than ingested into your context window.
15: 
16: ## Decision Tree: Choosing Your Approach
17: 
18: ```
19: User task → Is it static HTML?
20:     ├─ Yes → Read HTML file directly to identify selectors
21:     │         ├─ Success → Write Playwright script using selectors
22:     │         └─ Fails/Incomplete → Treat as dynamic (below)
23:     │
24:     └─ No (dynamic webapp) → Is the server already running?
25:         ├─ No → Run: python scripts/with_server.py --help
26:         │        Then use the helper + write simplified Playwright script
27:         │
28:         └─ Yes → Reconnaissance-then-action:
29:             1. Navigate and wait for networkidle
30:             2. Take screenshot or inspect DOM
31:             3. Identify selectors from rendered state
32:             4. Execute actions with discovered selectors
33: ```
34: 
35: ## Example: Using with_server.py
36: 
37: To start a server, run `--help` first, then use the helper:
38: 
39: **Single server:**
40: ```bash
41: python scripts/with_server.py --server "npm run dev" --port 5173 -- python your_automation.py
42: ```
43: 
44: **Multiple servers (e.g., backend + frontend):**
45: ```bash
46: python scripts/with_server.py \
47:   --server "cd backend && python server.py" --port 3000 \
48:   --server "cd frontend && npm run dev" --port 5173 \
49:   -- python your_automation.py
50: ```
51: 
52: To create an automation script, include only Playwright logic (servers are managed automatically):
53: ```python
54: from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
55: 
56: with sync_playwright() as p:
57:     browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True) # Always launch chromium in headless mode
58:     page = browser.new_page()
59:     page.goto('http://localhost:5173') # Server already running and ready
60:     page.wait_for_load_state('networkidle') # CRITICAL: Wait for JS to execute
61:     # ... your automation logic
62:     browser.close()
63: ```
64: 
65: ## Reconnaissance-Then-Action Pattern
66: 
67: 1. **Inspect rendered DOM**:
68:    ```python
69:    page.screenshot(path='/tmp/inspect.png', full_page=True)
70:    content = page.content()
71:    page.locator('button').all()
72:    ```
73: 
74: 2. **Identify selectors** from inspection results
75: 
76: 3. **Execute actions** using discovered selectors
77: 
78: ## Common Pitfall
79: 
80: ❌ **Don't** inspect the DOM before waiting for `networkidle` on dynamic apps
81: ✅ **Do** wait for `page.wait_for_load_state('networkidle')` before inspection
82: 
83: ## Best Practices
84: 
85: - **Use bundled scripts as black boxes** - To accomplish a task, consider whether one of the scripts available in `scripts/` can help. These scripts handle common, complex workflows reliably without cluttering the context window. Use `--help` to see usage, then invoke directly. 
86: - Use `sync_playwright()` for synchronous scripts
87: - Always close the browser when done
88: - Use descriptive selectors: `text=`, `role=`, CSS selectors, or IDs
89: - Add appropriate waits: `page.wait_for_selector()` or `page.wait_for_timeout()`
90: 
91: ## Reference Files
92: 
93: - **examples/** - Examples showing common patterns:
94:   - `element_discovery.py` - Discovering buttons, links, and inputs on a page
95:   - `static_html_automation.py` - Using file:// URLs for local HTML
96:   - `console_logging.py` - Capturing console logs during automation

# Lofi Studio — Architecture Overview & Major Enhancements

Both servers have been analyzed, enhanced, and verified:
- **Port 3000** (`http://localhost:3000/`): The Node.js rendering engine (`server.mjs`) & updated fallback interface (`public/index.html`).
- **Port 3001** (`http://localhost:3001/`): The primary Next.js Studio application (`web/app/`) with the full interactive creator workstation.

---

## 1. Project Architecture & Understanding

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Frontend["Frontend Studio (Port 3001)"]
        UI["Next.js 16 App Router (web/app)"]
        Ambience["Procedural Web Audio Engine (Vinyl, Rain, Hiss)"]
        Vault["Studio Vault (History Drawer)"]
        Theme["Theme Engine (Obsidian Dark / Warm Light)"]
    end

    subgraph Backend["Backend Engine (Port 3000)"]
        Server["HTTP Server (server.mjs)"]

### How the System Works:
1. **Audio Synthesis Engine ([`generate.mjs`](file:///c:/Users/thann/Downloads/AntiGravity/ClaudeLoFiGenerator/generate.mjs))**:
   - Synthesizes 44.1 kHz, 16-bit WAV audio directly in pure JavaScript without external sample libraries.
   - Simulates Rhodes-style electric piano harmonics with tape wow/flutter modulation, lowpass RC filtering, and gentle analog saturation.

If you are looking for open-source GitHub projects, repositories, or tools to generate **Lofi-style, anime, or Pixar-inspired AI videos**, several key projects and categories match what you need. 

Because "Lofi video generators" usually combine **stable generation (for background loops/characters)**, **video styling (Anime/Pixar filters)**, and **animation frameworks**, the ecosystem is split into a few top-tier GitHub repositories:

---

### 1. Dedicated Open-Source AI Video Studios & Workspaces
If you want an all-in-one local app to generate stylized scenes, character sheets, and video loops:
* **[gongxings / kemeng-ai-anime-creation (Kmeng AI Animata)](https://github.com/gongxings/kemeng-ai-anime-creation)**[1]
  * **What it does:** A local-first open-source AI video creation studio[1]. 
  * **Style Support:** Built-in multi-style presets specifically supporting **Anime, 3D Game (Pixar-like), and Cinematic environments**[1]. 
  * **Features:** Generates consistent character sheets (solving the shifting character problem in AI art) and builds high-fidelity background scenes using text-to-video and image-to-video models[1].
* **[LakshmiSravyaVedantham / VideoAI](https://github.com/LakshmiSravyaVedantham/VideoAI)**[2]
  * **What it does:** A full-stack AI video generation application with a professional UI[2].
  * **Styles & Controls:** It integrates multiple open models (like CogVideoX, LTX Video, Stable Video Diffusion, and AnimateDiff) and features preset video styles including **Anime, Cartoon, and 3D Render**, alongside camera movement controls (pan, zoom, tracking)[2] ideal for Lofi-style background pans.

### 2. Turning Photos/Videos into Anime or Pixar Styles (Video Style Transfer)
If you already have a static Lofi background (like a room or a desk setup) or a video of a person and want to convert it into an **Anime or Pixar 3D style**:
* **[TachibanaYoshino / AnimeGANv3](https://github.com/TachibanaYoshino/AnimeGANv3)**[3]
  * **What it does:** The gold standard repository for converting real photos and videos into distinct animation styles.

  * **What it does:** Uses Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to transform real-life videos and selfies into anime format directly[4]. It provides easy-to-use scripts (`record.py` for live webcam or video processing)[4].

### 3. Motion & Animation Generators (For Lofi Loops)
Lofi videos typically rely on subtle, repeating ambient motions (e.g., rain falling, hair blowing, a character writing, or coffee steam rising). 
* **AnimateDiff-based ecosystem (Search GitHub for `AnimateDiff` / `ComfyUI-AnimateDiff-EvoContext`):** 
  * AnimateDiff is the underlying open-source framework used by most developers to inject smooth motion into static Stable Diffusion checkpoints. By combining AnimateDiff with a **LoRA trained on Pixar or Lofi Anime styles**, developers create seamless, loopable background animations ideal for Lofi hip-hop streams.
* **[AIComicBuilder](https://github.com/LingyiChen-AI/AIComicBuilder)** or **[Awesome-AI-Workflows](https://github.com/eachlabs/Awesome-AI-Workflows)**[5][6]
  * Great repositories containing pre-built ComfyUI / Python pipelines that chain text-to-image (for the Lofi room/character) and image-to-video (for subtle animations like blinking or rain).

If you prefer a quick web app instead of cloning a massive Python repository with heavy checkpoint downloads:

The search for "ffmpeg filter graph anime look pixar bloom glow" returned the following summary:
To achieve an **anime/Pixar-style look** featuring soft highlights, dreamy bloom, and vibrant, clean contrast using FFmpeg, you need a multi-stage filter graph (`-filter_complex`)[1]. 

A "bloom" or "glow" effect works best by:
1. Splitting the video stream.
2. Isolating and crushing the bright highlights (thresholding/curves).
3. Blurring those highlights heavily.
4. Screening or overlaying the blurred highlights back onto the original crisp video[2].
5. Enhancing saturation and contrast for that animated look.

Here is an advanced FFmpeg filter graph command designed to accomplish this:

### The FFmpeg Command

```bash
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -filter_complex "
[0:v]split=2[orig][bloom];
[bloom]eq=brightness=0.08:contrast=1.3:saturation=1.4,curves=r='0/0 0.5/0.6 1/1':g='0/0 0.5/0.6 1/1':b='0/0 0.5/0.7 1/1'[bloom];
[bloom]gblur=sigma=25:steps=3[bloom];
[orig][bloom]blend=all_mode='screen':all_opacity=0.6[v];
[v]unsharp=5:5:0.8:3:3:0.4
" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a copy output.mp4
```

---

### Step-by-Step Breakdown of the Filter Graph

1. **`split=2[orig][bloom];`**
   * Takes your input video and splits it into two identical processing paths: one to stay sharp (`[orig]`) and one to turn into the glowing bloom layer (`[bloom]`)[3].

2. **`eq=...:curves=... [bloom];`**
   * **`eq`**: Boosts saturation (`1.4`) and contrast (`1.3`) to mimic the punchy, saturated color palettes typical of modern animation/Pixar styles.
   * **`curves`**: Gently lifts the mid-to-high tones (especially pushing the blue channel slightly higher) to give highlights that ethereal, cinematic anime glow.

3. **`gblur=sigma=25:steps=3 [bloom];`**
   * Applies a Gaussian blur to the processed bloom stream. A high `sigma` (e.g., `25`) spreads the light out wide. Adjust this number depending on your source resolution (use higher values like `40-50` for 4K video, or lower for 720p).

4. **`[orig][bloom]blend=all_mode='screen':all_opacity=0.6 [v];`**
   * Combines the original sharp video with the blurred glow layer using the **`screen`** blend mode[2]. Screen multiplication ensures highlights bloom brightly without washing out the dark areas into pure white. 
   * `all_opacity=0.6` controls how intense the glow is. Lower it to `0.3` for a subtle touch, or raise it to `0.8` for a dreamy fantasy sequence.

5. **`unsharp=5:5:0.8:3:3:0.4`**
   * *Optional final touch:* Animation typically features crisp, clean lines. A mild unsharp mask at the very end restores edge definition that might have been softened by the blur layer.

### Tips for Fine-Tuning:
* **For a stronger "Pixar 3D" feel:** Increase saturation further (`saturation=1.6`) and lower the gamma slightly.
* **For a retro 90s Anime look:** Add a slight color shift using `rgbashift`[4] or lower the `unsharp` strength to mimic traditional cel-shaded softness.

content:
### 1. Understanding Anime & Pixar Aesthetic Videos (Web & GitHub Research)

In the ecosystem of AI and procedural video generators (such as [AnimeGANv3](https://github.com/TachibanaYoshino/AnimeGANv3), [VideoAI](https://github.com/LakshmiSravyaVedantham/VideoAI), [Kmeng AI Animata](https://github.com/gongxings/kemeng-ai-anime-creation), and [AnimateDiff](https://github.com/guoyww/AnimateDiff)), **Anime** and **Pixar** represent two distinct visual and audio paradigms:

| Aesthetic Dimension | **Anime Cel Style** (Shinkai / Ghibli) | **Pixar Bloom Style** (3D Feature Animation) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Visual Architecture** | 2D hand-painted / cel-shaded Japanese animation. Sharp, clean outlines, high saturation, vivid sky gradients (violet, amber, rose), and dramatic natural light. | 3D CGI stylized animation with soft depth of field, volumetric warm lighting, plush surface textures (knits, fur, wood), and subsurface scattering skin glow. |
| **Post-Processing / Shaders** | Edge contrast accentuation (`unsharp`), cel color curves, high color saturation (`eq=saturation=1.42:contrast=1.16`), and gentle vignette. | Multi-path highlight isolation, wide-sigma Gaussian diffusion (`gblur`), screen blending (`blend=all_mode=screen:all_opacity=0.45`), and warm golden color balance. |
| **Musical Harmony** | **Royal Road Progression** ($F^{\text{maj7}} \rightarrow G^7 \rightarrow Em^7 \rightarrow Am^7$) popular in Joe Hisaishi and Makoto Shinkai anime films, paired with emotional piano and mellow beats. | Whimsical music box / celesta bells, warm storytelling chord voicings ($C^{\text{maj7}} \rightarrow F^{\text{maj7}} \rightarrow Dm^7 \rightarrow G^7$), and cozy fireplace Rhodes chords. |

---

### 2. Implementation in Our Web App

#### A. New Dedicated Master Artwork Assets ([`public/backgrounds/`](file:///c:/Users/thann/Downloads/AntiGravity/ClaudeLoFiGenerator/public/backgrounds))
We generated and added 4 high-definition scenes to the studio collection:
1. `anime_shinkai_sunset.jpg` — **Shinkai Twilight Train**: Makoto Shinkai twilight train carriage looking out at vibrant clouds, Tokyo skyline, and drifting cherry blossoms.
2. `pixar_cozy_cabin.jpg` — **Pixar Fireplace Cabin**: 3D Pixar animated cabin with a cozy character sipping cocoa by a roaring fireplace with a sleeping golden puppy.
3. `anime_ghibli_garden.jpg` — **Ghibli Summer Porch**: Hand-painted Studio Ghibli countryside porch overlooking blooming wildflowers, butterflies, and a snoozing calico cat.
4. `pixar_rooftop_stars.jpg` — **Pixar Rooftop Stargazing**: 3D Pixar animated twilight rooftop with vintage brass telescope, chunky scarf, and fluffy white cat under twinkling stars.

#### B. Advanced Multi-Stage Compositor Filters ([`server.mjs`](file:///c:/Users/thann/Downloads/AntiGravity/ClaudeLoFiGenerator/server.mjs))
Updated `STYLE_FILTERS` in the backend compositor:
- **Pixar Bloom (`style: "pixar"`):**
  ```bash
  [bg0]split=2[orig][bloom];
  [bloom]eq=brightness=0.06:contrast=1.28:saturation=1.45,gblur=sigma=20:steps=2[bloom];
  [orig][bloom]blend=all_mode=screen:all_opacity=0.45[blended];
  [blended]colorbalance=rs=0.05:gs=0.02:bs=-0.03,unsharp=5:5:0.7:3:3:0.3[bg]
  ```
- **Anime Cel (`style: "anime"`):**
  ```bash
  [bg0]hqdn3d=3:2:5:4,eq=saturation=1.42:contrast=1.16:brightness=0.02,
  unsharp=7:7:1.3:5:5:0.5,curves=r='0/0 0.5/0.52 1/1':b='0/0 0.5/0.54 1/1'[bg]
  ```

#### C. Harmonic Mood Additions ([`generate.mjs`](file:///c:/Users/thann/Downloads/AntiGravity/ClaudeLoFiGenerator/generate.mjs))
Added dedicated chord voicings and tempo setups:
- `shinkai_anime`: 78 BPM, $F^{\text{maj7}} \rightarrow G^7 \rightarrow Em^7 \rightarrow Am^7$ (Shinkai anime piano chords & radiant sunset breeze).
- `pixar_cozy`: 72 BPM, $C^{\text{maj7}} \rightarrow F^{\text{maj7}} \rightarrow Dm^7 \rightarrow G^7$ (Pixar 3D hearth warmth & storybook chimes).
- `ghibli_garden`: 74 BPM, $C^{\text{maj7}} \rightarrow Em^7 \rightarrow F^{\text{maj7}} \rightarrow G^7$ (Summer country porch acoustic calm).

#### D. Frontend Studio UI ([`web/app/page.tsx`](file:///c:/Users/thann/Downloads/AntiGravity/ClaudeLoFiGenerator/web/app/page.tsx) & [`public/index.html`](file:///c:/Users/thann/Downloads/AntiGravity/ClaudeLoFiGenerator/public/index.html))
- Added dedicated quick inspiration chips:
  - 🌸 **Shinkai Twilight (Anime)**
  - ✨ **Pixar Fireplace (Pixar)**
  - 🍃 **Ghibli Garden (Anime)**
  - 🔭 **Pixar Stargazing (Pixar)**
- Added **Style Badges** (`Anime`, `Pixar 3D`, `Lofi`) to the scene selection cards.
- Integrated auto-pairing: selecting a visual style card automatically selects matching scene artwork and harmonic voicings.

---

### 3. Verification & Test Runs

All 4 combinations were generated, inspected, and verified:

| Test Run | Style | Mood | Scene Artwork | Video ID | Output & Verification |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Anime Shinkai** | `anime` | `shinkai_anime` | `anime_shinkai_sunset.jpg` | `#58eb89ef` | Clean cel outlines, radiant twilight clouds, Tokyo tower, live audio wave. |
| **Pixar Cabin** | `pixar` | `pixar_cozy` | `pixar_cozy_cabin.jpg` | `#dbe1a08d` | Volumetric warm bloom, 3D character with cocoa, sleeping puppy, fireplace glow. |
| **Ghibli Garden** | `anime` | `ghibli_garden` | `anime_ghibli_garden.jpg` | `#5c7839cd` | Hand-painted watercolor porch, blooming wildflowers, calico cat, summer breeze. |
| **Pixar Rooftop** | `pixar` | `dreamy` | `pixar_rooftop_stars.jpg` | `#146f0661` | Soft 3D depth of field, string fairy lights, telescope & fluffy white cat under starry sky. |
